approved: Criminal Code Amendment (Sharing of Abhorrent Violent Material) Bill 2019
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
The bill would create new criminal offences for internet, content and hosting services that fail to act quickly to remove or stop hosting abhorrent violent material accessible in Australia.

Service providers who become aware of such material would have to refer details to the Australian Federal Police within a reasonable time, and content or hosting services would also have to remove or stop hosting the material.
The eSafety Commissioner could issue a notice to a content or hosting service stating that abhorrent violent material was accessible or hosted on its service at the time of the notice.
Introduces Commonwealth offences for failing to refer abhorrent violent material to the AFP within a reasonable time.
Introduces Commonwealth offences for failing to remove or cease hosting abhorrent violent material accessible in Australia.
Gives the eSafety Commissioner power to issue a notice to a content or hosting service about abhorrent violent material.
Internet service providers, content service providers and hosting service providers.

The majority voted against a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debates/?id=2019-04-04.15.1) that would have amended the usual [second reading](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html) motion: *That the majority agree with the bill's main idea.* Or, in parliamentary jargon, "*That this bill be now read a second time.*" ### Motion text > *That all words after "That" be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:* > *"whilst not declining to give the bill a second reading, the House refers the bill to the [Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Committees/Joint/Intelligence_and_Security) for inquiry and report no later than 1 August 2019".* ### What does the bill do? The [explanatory memorandum](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Fems%2Fs1201_ems_08b22f92-a323-4512-bf31-bc55aab31a81%22;rec=0) explained that: > *The Christchurch terrorist attack on 15 March 2019 demonstrated the potential for live streaming and other video sharing platforms to be abused by extremist perpetrators to amplify their messages in the immediate aftermath of these incidents. In that case, the perpetrator streamed the attack in real-time. The video was then widely re-shared across a number of social media platforms.* > > *The Criminal Code Amendment (Sharing of Abhorrent Violent Material) Bill 2019 (Bill) will address significant gaps in Australia’s current criminal laws by ensuring that persons who are internet service providers, or who provide content or hosting services, take timely action in relation to abhorrent violent material that can be accessed using their services. This will ensure that online platforms cannot be exploited and weaponised by perpetrators of violence.*

The speaker introduced the Criminal Code Amendment (Sharing of Abhorrent Violent Material) Bill, requiring internet platforms to expeditiously remove abhorrent violent material and notify the Australian Federal Police, with penalties of up to $2.1 million or three years imprisonment for individuals and $10.5 million or 10% of annual turnover for corporations. The bill was presented in response to the Christchurch terrorist attack of 15 March 2019, where footage was live-streamed and remained on Facebook for nearly an hour and ten minutes.

Labor will support the Criminal Code Amendment (Sharing of Abhorrent Violent Material) Bill 2019 despite calling it clumsy and flawed, citing problems including potential conflict with US law, privacy risks, impact on whistleblowing, arbitrary distinctions between broadcasters and online platforms, and lack of resources for enforcement. The speaker also criticised the Morrison government for rushing the bill without proper consultation and for its past attacks on section 18C of the Racial Discrimination Act and deals with One Nation.

The Greens MP argued that the Criminal Code Amendment (Sharing of Abhorrent Violent Material) Bill 2019 was being rushed through parliament without proper scrutiny, risking unintended consequences such as criminalising journalism, and moved an amendment to refer the bill to the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security for inquiry and report by 1 August 2019.

The speaker argued that the Criminal Code Amendment (Sharing of Abhorrent Violent Material) Bill 2019 should not be rushed through parliament, citing unclear definitions like "expeditious," risks to whistleblowers and media, and the need for a public interest defence, and called for referral to a parliamentary committee for review.
